PAPER: Artificial Intelligence Review (2026) 59:28 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11445-x A critical review of explainable deep learning in lung cancer diagnosis Emmanouil Koutoulakis1,2 · Eleftherios Trivizakis1 · Emmanouil Markodimitrakis1,2 · Sophia Agelaki3,4 · Manolis Tsiknakis1,2 · Kostas Marias1,2 Received: 29 July 2025 / Accepted: 30 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract In the current research landscape, there is a plethora of artificial intelligence methods for medical image analysis, improving diagnostic accuracy; however, AI introduces challeng- es related to trustworthiness and transparency of decisions. Clinicians and medical experts often find it difficult to comprehend the process by which machine learning models arrive at specific outcomes. This has the potential to hinder the ethical use of AI in a clinical set- ting. Explainable AI (XAI) enables clinicians to interpret and consequently improve trust for outcomes predicted by ML models. This review critically examines emerging trends in XAI applied to lung cancer modeling. Novel XAI implementations in tasks like weakly supervised lesion localization, prognostic models, and survival analysis are highlighted. Furthermore, this study explores the extend of clinician contributions in the development of XAI, the impact of interobserver variability, the evaluation and scoring of explanation maps, the adaptation of XAI methods to medical imaging, and lung-specific attributes that may influence XAI. Novel extensions to the current state-of-the-art are also discussed critically throughout this study. However, contemporary AI models often comprise millions to billions of learned param- eters, functioning as black boxes regarding their decision-making processes (Trivizakis et al. 2020). In particular, the explainability of an AI decision is a critical issue in the medical field since in the current clinical practice a therapeutic strategy is decided through standard- ized protocols and international standards, such as specific markers from laboratory and clinical data, medical images, molecular markers, or extensive reporting systems. The lack of transparency in the current deep learning (DL) models is limiting the trust and adoption from the clinicians (Sagona et al. 2025). Consequently, the accountability of AI in clinical settings remains a concern, as the absence of a comprehensive explainability framework undermines clinical translation, patient safety, and regulatory compliance. Lung cancer has the highest mortality rate among all other cancers, according to the World Health Organization (Latest Global Cancer Data: Cancer Burden Rises to 18.1 million New Cases and 9.6 Million Cancer Deaths in 2018 – IARC 2025; World Health Organization (WHO), "Lung Cancer" 2025). This type of cancer is characterized by high heterogeneity in various parameters that significantly affect therapeutic strategies, including lesion size, stage, morphology, growth dynamics, genetic variability, and molecular subtypes (Triviza- kis et al. 2021). Additionally, the genotypic or pathological nature of the microenvironment, as well as the health status of the organ, are crucial factors that remain underexplored in the current literature. To holistically model such complex lesions, multimodal data integration has emerged as a critical strategy in recent studies (Trivizakis et al. 2023; Hassan et al. 2024; Farooq et al. 2025; Lu et al. 2025). The current explainability and interpretability methods for deep learning models lack comprehensiveness and completeness in the context of XAI use in clinical practice (Mar- tinho et al. 2021). The vast majority of the proposed XAI methods in the literature focus primarily on visualizing low-level spatial features (Patrício et al. 2023), attention maps (Tsiknakis et al. 2020), or rank raw deep filters/features (Trivizakis et al. 2023) from the examined regions of interest. In particular, methods such as occlusion (Zeiler and Fergus 2014) generate maps that show which sub-regions of the image influence the examined class. The integrated gradients (IG) (Wargnier-Dauchelle et al. 2021) calculate a supple- mentary average gradient by differing the input in conjunction with a specified initial state. Guided back propagation (GBP) (Springenberg et al. 2014) assumes that artificial neurons function as feature detectors; therefore, a set of activated neurons is selected and their output is mapped to the original image, showing the regions with the most significant features for a specific class. DeconvNet (Sundararajan et al. 2017) premise is founded on reversing the deep network’s information flow (feature maps) to identify the activations across all layers and map them to the input image. Many variations of gradient-weighted class activation mapping (GradCAM) (Chattopadhay et al. 2018; Zhao et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2019; Sel- varaju et al. 2020) have been proposed as a post-hoc interpretability solution. 1 3 28 Page 4 of 38 E. Generally, interpretations based on visualizations are widely used in medical image analysis tasks because they are easy to implement (e.g., post-hoc, model agnostic) and are intuitive in showing the important regions from which the decision was deduced. Nonetheless, clinicians often disagree when qualitatively assessing specific endpoints or interpretability visualizations, a challenge known as inter-observer variability (Tsiknakis et al. 2020), which may hinder the adaptation of XAI, as many still rely on ambiguous or poorly defined visualizations. Additionally, the methods presented in the current literature often overlook key features critical for medical applications such as semantic, anatomical, regional, local, and global imaging characteristics, as well as quantitative metrics or other lesion-specific attributes. Therefore, these techniques are not specifically designed for the medical field but are derivatives of interpretability methods originally developed for natural image analysis. Specifi- cally, prior works have rarely investigated the role of clinicians in the development stage of XAI or assessed its clinical applicability and reliability. F ig. 4 Modalities used in the reviewed studies A saliency map (Simonyan et al. 2013) is a visualization that highlights regions of the input image that are most influential to the prediction of the model. Specifically, a saliency map is calculated by using a backpropagation-based approach, where the class score is adjusted based on the image or 3D volume, highlighting the pixels or voxels that most affect the class probability. The SmoothGrad (Smilkov et al. 2017) generates multiple noisy versions of an input image, computes a sensitivity map for each, and then averages these maps. This averaging process effectively smooths out false variations and highlights robust features the model deems important. Occlusion sensitivity mapping (Zeiler and Fergus 2013) systematically occludes various parts of an input image/volume and observes how the model’s output changes. In practice, a small patch window slides across the image or volume; at each position, the patch region is replaced with a baseline value, and the model’s prediction is recorded. Regions that cause the greatest drop in prediction accuracy are considered the most important to the decision- making process. Class activation mapping (CAM) (Zhou et al. 2015) integrates the structure of global average pooling (GAP) (Lin et al. 2013), providing a technique for visualizing the image regions a CNN uses for classification. An architecture that implements CAM, uses GAP at the final convolution layer to reduce a 2D feature map to a single average value. It works by taking a weighted average of the feature maps from the final convolutional layer, where the weights are derived from the connections leading to the output neuron for the class of interest. The resulting heatmap visually indicates which parts of the image the CNN finds the most influential when making its prediction. Gradient-weighted CAM (GradCAM) (Selvaraju et al. 2020) is a variation of CAM, creating heatmaps that highlight the important regions in an input image that the model used to predict/classify a specific class. Unlike the CAM, GradCAM is a generalization that does not require a specific network architecture (GAP followed by the output layer). It can be applied in a wide variety of CNN architectures. In particular, GradCAM focuses on the gradient information from the final convolution layer to understand the importance of each neuron to highlight the features that contributed to the decision-making. A refinement of GradCAM is the Guided-GradCAM, which is the product of GradCAM and Guided Backpropagation (Springenberg et al. 2014), offering high-resolution detail but not being class-discriminative. 1 3 A critical review of explainable deep learning in lung cancer diagnosis Page 9 of 38 28 GradCAM++ (Chattopadhay et al. 2018) is an enhanced version of GradCAM. While GradCAM identifies important regions and each pixel’s gradient contributes equally to the overall importance score, GradCAM + + aims for better localization by introducing pixel- level weighting into the calculation of feature map importance. RespondCAM (Zhao et al. 2018) utilizes the gradients of a target class flowing into a convolutional layer. The gradients are used to weight the feature maps, which are then combined to generate a heatmap, highlighting the salient regions in the input image. The algorithm can be adapted to any CNN architecture efficiently, and it is particularly effective for 3D biomedical imaging data. GraphCAM (Zheng et al. 2022a) is inspired by transformer interpretability methods that analyze attention. It generates class-specific heatmaps by propagating relevance scores backward from the output class through the transformer’s attention layers. It computes a relevance map based on gradients and attention maps within the transformer, then maps this relevance from the pooled graph representation back to the original graph nodes using the pooling layer’s learned assignments, and finally reconstructs a spatial heatmap highlighting the important regions for a specific class prediction. ScoreCAM (Wang et al. 2019) is a gradient-free technique that visualizes the feature importance from a chosen convolution layer based on how much each activation map con- tributes to the model’s confidence score for a specific class. Due to its gradient-free nature, ScoreCAM often produces clearer and less noisy visualization compared to gradient-based techniques. Visual Backpropagation (VBP) (Zeiler and Fergus 2013; Springenberg et al. 2014) meth- odology aims to understand features learned within a CNN by mapping feature activations from higher layers back to the input pixel space. This is typically achieved using techniques like DeconvNets (Sundararajan et al. 2017) or Guided Backpropagation, which reverse or approximate the CNN’s forward operations. The process involves steps such as inverting filtering operations (often using transposed filters), reconstructing the signal through non- linearities like ReLU, and approximating the inverse of pooling operations. The resulting reconstruction highlights the input patterns or structures that most strongly stimulated the specific feature map being analyzed. Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) (Montavon et al. 2018) is a technique used to explain the predictions of DL models by determining the contribution of each input feature to the output. It operates via performing a backward pass, starting from the network’s output neuron, and progressively redistributing the prediction score layer by layer onto the input neurons, yielding relevance scores for the original input variables. Specific propagation rules are applied at each layer to divide the relevance among lower-layer neurons based on their contribution to the activations in the forward pass. Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) (Ribeiro et al. 2016) is a model-agnostic technique that focuses on accurately explaining why the model made the prediction for a single instance. Specifically, LIME works by generating multiple perturbed versions of the input image and inspecting how the prediction changed for these altered versions. Then, a simpler model was developed to mimic the complex model’s behavior for these specific perturbations, which highlights the parts of the original inputs that had the biggest impact on the decision. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) (Lundberg and Lee 2017) aim to explain the out- put of any machine learning model by calculating the contribution of each feature to the 1 3 28 Page 10 of 38 E. Koutoulakis et al. model’s prediction. It is based on game theory; specifically, it uses Shapley values to assign credit to each feature for how much it shifted the prediction from the average outcome. In particular, XAI approaches were identified based on their type (post-hoc, ante-hoc, and a combination of them) and their methodological attributes. According to the reviewed literature, most studies employed post-hoc explainability and primarily gradient-based methods due to their ease of implementation. However, there is a need for identification of optimal explainabil- ity technique since most of current implementations are highly task-dependent and lack methodological standarization. The decision-making process of the AI system needs to be 1 3 28 Page 24 of 38 E. Koutoulakis et al. dependable and trustworthy for medical prognosis. Without rigorous comparative frame- works that integrates the expertise of both researchers and clinicians, XAI risks remaining technically descriptive rather than clinically meaningful. For instance, GradCAM highlights general areas of attention, whereas SHAP offers more granular feature-specific insights into the model’s predictive behavior. 4.1 Comparison of XAI methods Standalone XAI methods can provide valuable insights into model attention, but they can lead to potential biases. The methodological bias inherent in each technique can result in different highlighted features, requiring a comparative approach for a comprehensive under- standing of the predictions, as shown by Fig. 6. A significant challenge identified in this review was the lack of systematic comparative analysis among XAI methods. Only a small group of the reviewed articles performed comparisons (Gu et al. 2020; Dehkharghanian et al. 2021; Saihood et al. 2023), highlighting the need for an advanced evaluation to deter- mine the reliability of different explanations. This observation underlines a deeper research bottleneck of interpretability remaining method-dependent and disjointed across different studies. Although, the use of interpretabil- ity techniques advances transparency, the lack of standardized comparisons with specific metrics and qualitative assessments limits the ability of evaluating the most reliable and intuitive XAI method. A great example is depicted in Fig. 6, where Dehkharganian et al. compared multiple post-hoc XAI methods showing the visualization variabilities. Without such comparative analysis, there is a risk of misinterpretation, especially in critical domains like medical diag- nosis and prognosis, where reliability and trustworthiness are common concerns for clinical F ig. 6 Example of visual comparison among multiple XAI methods (Deh- kharghanian et al. 2021) 1 3 A critical review of explainable deep learning in lung cancer diagnosis Page 25 of 38 28 use. Additionally, the authors conclude that different interpretability methods can pos- sibly produce different feature importance, which may suggest a potential selection bias at the attention map level. 4.2 Quantitative evaluation of XAI method XAI was designed to qualitatively identify potential issues and regions of attention of the converged models, attempting to interpret the outcomes of the model. Zheng et al. (2024) and Hasan et al. (2024) assessed both quantitatively and qualitatively their explainability of their methods using evaluation metrics such as Dice, nRMSE, SSIM, and MS-SSIM to highlight potential bias of the weighted attention of a model; however, using such metrics is an oversimplification of an intricate task like the explainability of a deep learning models. Furthermore, the reliance on proxy metrics created to measure the spatial overlap rather than the quality of an interpretation has the potential of misrepresenting the explanatory value of XAI and produce misguided conclusions. The absence of consensus on a proper interpretability score consist a major limiting factor of these studies, hampering reproducibility and comparability of XAI methods performance. On the other hand, some studies (Cui et al. 2020b; Lin et al. 2021; Higuchi et al. 2023; Mercaldo et al. 2024; Hermoza et al. 2024; Kim et al. 2024) are utilizing interpretabil- ity methods as weakly supervised segmentation or lesion localization methods. This shifts XAI role from explaining the decision-making process to serving as a proxy for annotation, potentially blurring the line between interpretation and prediction. 4.3 Involvement of clinical experts Clinical involvement is essential for validating XAI outputs. Studies that incorporated clini- cal feedback, either through direct interpretation or by indirect evaluation against expert annotations, provided an additional layer of validation. These studies are presented in Table 4. However, the level and quality of clinical involvement varied, with some studies relying on a single expert (Di et al. 2023) or multiple (Cui et al. 2020b), other studies used struc- tured scoring systems (Dehkharghanian et al. 2021; Verma et al. 2024), or indirectly used pathologists’ annotations (Lu et al. 2021; Chen et al. 2024; Hermoza et al. 2024; Kabiraj et al. 2024). These differentiations on leveraging experts during research highlights the need for enhanced clinician engagement as an integral part of the XAI development instead of a background role. In the absence of clinician-guided interpretation and recurrent feedback mechanisms, XAI outputs may be technically coherent yet clinically insignificant. 1 3 28 Page 26 of 38 E. Koutoulakis et al. Moreover, the lack of research addressing interobserver variability in XAI (Fig. 7), potentially leading to inconsistencies in understanding the decision-making process of the model. In particular, a single expert opinion has a high risk of over-reliance, possibly creat- ing a false sense of confidence in an XAI method’s performance and explainability. Mul- tiple observers could potentially alleviate such biases. This may require the adaptation of a standardized evaluation method with multiple observers and specific criteria during the evaluation of XAI methods. Quantifying and addressing this variability with multi-observer scoring systems are necessary to improve the trustworthiness of AI for a wide clinical adoption. 4.4 Confounding variables that potentially affect XAI As for attributes that affect XAI, such as comorbidities, complex tissue patterns, imaging artifacts, and other pulmonary lesions, these can potentially degrade the interpretability of AI models by capturing or shifting the attention of the model. Most of the examined studies focused on model design and the engineering part of the XAI techniques, while a smaller number addressed these medical attributes (Cui et al. 2020b; Dehkharghanian et al. 2021; Liang et al. 2024; Verma et al. 2024). Contemporary state-of-the-art methods are optimized for curated datasets featuring clean imaging data, as opposed to the heterogeneous “real-world” clinical sites. In par- ticular, excluding a subgroup of patients with comorbidities during the development of a model can improve performance, but the model does capture characteristics of prospec- tive patient cohorts, making it unfit for clinical practice. “Real-world” applications will implicitly include more complex clinical cases that will affect the model’s predictive power and interpretability. Cui et al. (2020b) excluded 144 participants with a medical history of tuberculosis from their study, reducing clinical trust and utility. In contrast, Verma et al. (2024) mentioned the fact that artifacts such as patient movements or breathing during the screening process can cause imperfection or distortions, resulting in false-positive cases and biased attention maps. Another variable that is discussed is the impact of magnifica- tion levels of the input images. Optimizing image representation can lead to a robust and interpretable AI system that allows more granular understanding and explainability. Liang et al. (2022b, 2024) developed a graph-based CAM technique designed for WSI analysis. GraphCAM computes the class activation maps by propagating gradients and rel- evance from the model’s output class directly to the input graph space, then reconstructs the final saliency map for the WSI from its graph representation. This consists of an evolution- ary improvement of current XAI methods from being generic visual aids to domain-specific as biologically explainable systems. The mapping of relevant features within the graph space, accompanied by high-level semantics, establishes contextual and causal connections for joint analysis and interpret- ability. The use of GraphCAM enhances visual explanations, aligning more closely with the complex biological and clinical realities. A major concern is the lack of causality between the underlying learned features and model outcomes (Liu et al. 2020; Dehkharghanian et al. 2021). Authors also highlight the limited decision transparency (Yang et al. 2021), XAI method biases (Chaunzwa et al. 2021; Shim et al. 2021; Kumaran et al. 2024), interpret- ability challenges with explainability maps (Shim et al. 2021; Di et al. 2023; Zhu et al. 2023; Kabiraj et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024), and imbalanced or size-limited testing datasets (Mercaldo et al. 2024; Lin et al. 2021; Mukashyaka et al. 2024; Liang et al. 2024). The poor quality of tumor localization (Hermoza et al. 2024; Kabiraj et al. 2024) and segmentation performance (Lu et al. 2021) has been highlighted in studies that weakly supervised models used XAI methods to perform the localization tasks. There exists poten- tial for innovative application of XAI in oncology by utilizing the diverse array of informa- tion intrinsic to this domain (imaging, clinical data, semantics, reports, omics, etc.). Ante-hoc, hybrid methodologies, and alternative XAI techniques are underutilized in lung cancer research, potentially skewing the conclusions of a comparative study. Inherently embedded mechanisms may enhance transparency throughout model convergence, facili- tating a more accurate assessment of model quality. Furthermore, the design of systematic comparative evaluations employing a diverse set of interpretability methods across identical or similar datasets and tasks will highlight the strengths and biases of specific XAI methods. Enhanced clinician involvement will facilitate the integration of XAI, foster trust in AI, and potentially boost the adoption of such methods in the clinical practice. Standardized scoring systems and rigorous criteria for assessing these frameworks will mitigate the risk of biased interpretation. Multi-expert research should examine and quantify interobserver variability in differ- ent analysis tasks, XAI methods, and clinical endpoints by employing statistical models to capture clinicians’ interpretations of XAI outputs, thereby influencing the development of intuitive explanatory visualizations. Clinical and imaging confounders, including acquisition variability, scanner-dependent pixel intensity distributions, imaging artifacts, lung comorbidities, must be incorporated into the design and assessment of novel XAI methodologies. Moreover, incorporating mul- timodality in XAI would align interpretations with the fundamental biological and clinical variables alongside the visual cues in imaging data. The introduction of causal explainability in the current state-of-the-art techniques will advance beyond basic correlation-based interpretations by incorporating counterfactual rea- soning, causal inference, and interpretability grounded in medical knowledge. Current literature lacks standardized interpretability benchmarks specifically pertaining to oncology. While substantial progress has been made in applying XAI in lung cancer models, current research remains dominated by post-hoc, gradient-based methods that lack causal and clinically rel- evant interpretation. There is a pressing need for standardized and systematic evaluation frameworks of XAI techniques that combine qualitative and quantitative metrics, deeper clinical involvement in both development and validation, and a clearer understanding of how specific medical attributes, such as comorbidities, image artifacts, and interobserver variability, impact interpretability. Emerging hybrid and causal-enhanced approaches may offer advances in XAI but currently reproducibility and rigorous clinical validation should be the focus. Addressing these methodological and translational challenges through caus- ally informed and domain-aware systems will be essential to enhancing XAI from a visual interpretation tool into a clinically reliable in silico expert in precision oncology. JSON: Name: xai_lung_benchmark_ensemble Title: A standardized multi-method evaluation framework and clinician-anchored benchmark for robust explainable deep learning in lung cancer imaging Short Hypothesis: A consensus explanation produced by ensembling complementary XAI methods will achieve significantly higher agreement with a multi-expert clinical reference (measured by localization IoU/Dice and blinded clinician relevance ratings) and greater robustness under acquisition and artifact stress tests than any single XAI method. Related Work: Existing work on explainable deep learning in lung cancer primarily relies on post-hoc gradient-based visualization methods (CAM family, GradCAM/GradCAM++, Guided-GradCAM), perturbation and gradient-aggregation techniques (Integrated Gradients, SmoothGrad, Guided Backpropagation), feature-importance methods (LRP, SHAP, LIME), attention-based heatmaps and weakly supervised MIL attention, and recent graph/transformer-based saliency (GraphCAM). Ante-hoc interpretable models and hybrid neuro-probabilistic approaches exist but are rare. Prior studies commonly apply a single XAI method, report qualitative examples, and occasionally use simplistic spatial overlap metrics; few conduct systematic multi-method comparisons, multi-expert evaluations, or standardized stress tests. Limitations across prior work include method-dependent and inconsistent explanations, scarce clinician-in-the-loop scoring or multi-observer variability analysis, inadequate robustness testing to scanner/vendor/windowing/artifacts, sparse open benchmarks with multi-reader localized annotations, and the absence of reproducible evaluation protocols to compare XAI reliability and clinical relevance. Abstract: We propose a standardized evaluation framework and multi-observer benchmark to measure and improve the clinical reliability of explainable AI (XAI) for lung cancer imaging. The framework integrates a curated multi-modality dataset (CT, chest radiograph, and whole-slide histopathology) with multi-expert localized annotations, blinded clinician relevance ratings, and a battery of acquisition and artifact stress tests. We implement and compare a diverse panel of XAI methods (gradient-based, perturbation-based, feature-importance, attention and graph-based) and introduce ensemble consensus strategies that aggregate complementary explanations into a unified saliency output. Evaluation uses spatial localization metrics, image-similarity and perturbation-robustness scores, and interobserver agreement statistics. Primary contributions are (1) an open, clinician-anchored benchmark and stress-test protocol for lung-cancer XAI, (2) reproducible evaluation metrics and reporting guidelines, and (3) demonstration that multi-method ensembles calibrated with clinician scores produce more accurate and robust explanations than single methods. Expected impact is to enable fair comparison of XAI techniques and accelerate clinically trustworthy adoption of interpretable deep learning in oncology. Experiments: Datasets: LIDC-IDRI (CT nodules with multilabel annotations), publicly available chest X-ray dataset with nodule/lesion localization (e.g., ChestX-ray14 or CheXpert extended with localization), TCGA LUAD/LUSC whole-slide images (WSIs) with tumor region annotations; plus a held-out multi-center clinical cohort (private) for external validation. Annotation protocol: derive per-scan/patch localization masks from 3–5 independent expert readers (radiologists for CT/CXR, pathologists for WSI); collect blinded 5-point clinician relevance ratings for each generated explanation. XAI methods (baselines): CAM, GradCAM, GradCAM++, ScoreCAM, SmoothGrad, Guided Backpropagation, Integrated Gradients, LRP, SHAP (image-adapted), LIME, attention-based MIL heatmaps, GraphCAM. Proposed comparators: (A) single-method outputs; (B) simple average ensemble of normalized saliency maps; (C) weighted ensemble calibrated via clinician relevance scores; (D) ensemble excluding perturbation-based methods (ablation). Evaluation metrics: localization IoU and Dice between saliency-thresholded maps and expert masks; SSIM/nRMSE/MS-SSIM between maps and clinician-derived probability maps; rank correlation (Spearman) and mean absolute difference with clinician relevance ratings; AOPC/AUC of perturbation tests (area over perturbation curve); robustness delta under stress tests (vendor shift, CT window shifts, simulated motion/respiratory artifacts, added text/markers); interobserver agreement (Fleiss kappa) for clinician ratings; statistical tests: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank for method comparisons, bootstrap 95% CI for metric differences. Experimental setup: 5-fold cross-validation on internal/train sets, final evaluation on held-out multi-center cohort. Ablations: compare ensembles with and without clinician calibration; remove each XAI family type in turn to measure contribution; compare ante-hoc interpretable model outputs (where available) against post-hoc ensembles. Reproducibility: fix random seeds, report per-fold results, and release code and evaluation scripts. Risk Factors and Limitations: Annotation bias and ambiguity: multi-expert masks may disagree and produce noisy ground truth for localization metrics; clinician ratings are subjective and may show high interobserver variability. Dataset generalization: public benchmarks and private cohorts may not capture full vendor, protocol, or population diversity; external validity may be limited. Computational cost: running many XAI methods and perturbation-based tests across large WSIs is resource intensive and may limit scale. Ensemble collapse: aggregating methods could amplify common systematic biases rather than correct them, producing misleading consensus explanations. Metric limitations: spatial overlap and image-similarity metrics may not reflect clinical usefulness or causal relevance of explanations. Confounders: models and XAI outputs may latch onto non-disease cues (markers, laterality text, comorbid patterns) that survive stress tests and mislead evaluation. Scalability: clinician-in-the-loop calibration and multi-reader studies are time-consuming and may limit dataset size. Regulatory and privacy constraints may restrict sharing of some clinical cohorts.
